screens.title: Advanced DynamoDB Features and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore the advanced capabilities of DynamoDB that let you support complex queries, extreme read performance, and safe multi-item updates. You'll learn when to choose Local Secondary Indexes for alternative sort orders within a partition, and when Global Secondary Indexes let you query by entirely different keys across the table. We'll also examine DynamoDB Accelerator, an in-memory cache for read-heavy workloads, and DynamoDB Transactions for grouping related updates with ACID guarantees. Finally, you'll see how DynamoDB Streams enable event-driven patterns such as search-index updates and real-time analytics. Each section pairs conceptual guidance with concrete examples and a short Python demo pattern. By the end you'll be able to map common access patterns — like finding users by email, transferring funds between accounts, or pushing updates to a search index — to the right DynamoDB feature. A quick misconception check: eventual consistency applies to GSIs and caches like DAX, so if you need immediate strong consistency you will prefer LSIs or specific read strategies. Consider this orientation your roadmap: pick the right index for the access pattern, use DAX for read scale when eventual consistency is acceptable, use transactions when operations must be atomic, and use Streams to integrate DynamoDB into event-driven pipelines.

screens.title: LSI vs GSI — what changes and what stays the same
screens.narratorSegment: Indexes let you query attributes other than the table primary key, but LSIs and GSIs differ in important respects. A Local Secondary Index shares the table partition key and provides a different sort key, so it's local to items that share a partition value and always offers strong consistency with the base table. Because of that close coupling, LSIs must be defined when you create the table. A Global Secondary Index can have an entirely different partition key and sort key, letting queries span the whole table across partitions, and you can add or remove GSIs after table creation. GSIs are by default eventually consistent, and they have separate capacity or on-demand billing configurations. Practically, use an LSI when you need alternative sorting for items within the same partition and you require strong consistency. Use a GSI when you need to support a different access pattern — for example, finding users by email or items by category across the entire dataset. A common misconception is to think GSIs are always a drop-in replacement for LSIs; they are not, because GSIs may return stale results briefly and consume separate capacity. Key decision factors are your access patterns, consistency requirements, and whether you can design keys up front. Think in terms of query needs first, then index to support them.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › LSI vs GSI
Local Secondary Index (LSI)
Same partition key, different sort key; strong consistency within partition; defined at table creation.
Use case: Query a user's orders by date when user_id is the partition key.
Behavior: Consistent reads reflect the base table immediately within that partition.
Constraint: Cannot add after table creation.
Common mistake
Expecting LSIs to scale across partitions — they are limited to items sharing the same partition key value.
Global Secondary Index (GSI)
Different partition and sort key allowed; queries span all partitions; eventually consistent by default; can be added later.
Use case: Query users by email across the entire Users table.
Behavior: Might lag briefly after writes — design for eventual consistency.
Operation: Has separate capacity or on-demand billing settings.
Practical tip
When adding a GSI for a new access pattern, seed the attribute values on existing items or re-write items to populate the index.
Consistency
LSI: strong within partition. GSI: eventual by default.
Lifecycle
LSI: create with table. GSI: can be added or removed later.
Cost & Capacity
GSIs consume separate capacity; LSIs consume base table capacity.

screens.title: Local Secondary Index (LSI) deep dive
screens.narratorSegment: A Local Secondary Index provides an alternate sort key while keeping the table's partition key. This relationship makes LSIs local to the partition key value, so queries using the LSI only see items that share that partition. Because the index is tightly coupled to the base table, reads through an LSI are strongly consistent with the base table, and changes are reflected immediately for that partition. LSIs are most appropriate when you know you will query items under the same partition in different orderings — for example, storing orders with user_id as partition key and using order_date as an LSI sort key to list a user's orders by date. Remember that LSIs must be created at table creation time, so include them in your initial schema design if you need this behavior. A common design trap is attempting to use an LSI to support queries across partitions; LSIs cannot do that because their partition key is the table partition key. In practice you would model user-scoped queries with LSIs and use GSIs when queries must span all users. Key takeaway: LSIs give immediate, strongly consistent alternate sorting inside a partition, but they require forward schema planning.

keyIdea.title: LSI core fact
keyIdea.text: LSIs are for alternative sort keys scoped to a partition and provide strong consistency, but must be chosen at table creation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Local Secondary Index
Definition
An index that uses the same partition key as the base table but a different sort key.
  • • Strong consistency for reads within a partition because the index is local to that partition.
  • • Must be defined at table creation; cannot be added later.
  • • Useful for alternative ordering or projecting different attributes within a partition.
Concrete example
If a table has user_id as the partition key and order_id as the sort key, add an LSI with user_id and order_date to query a user's orders by date without scanning.
Why it matters
Strongly consistent, low-latency queries inside a partition help build predictable user-scoped views.
Gotchas
LSIs count against the table's storage and capacity behavior; design them early if required by access patterns.

screens.title: Global Secondary Index (GSI) deep dive
screens.narratorSegment: A Global Secondary Index gives you the freedom to query a table using a different partition key and sort key than the base table. Because GSIs are global, queries on them can return items from across all partitions, enabling entirely new access patterns such as looking up accounts by status or users by email. GSIs can be added or removed after table creation and have their own capacity or on-demand billing configurations. The trade-off is eventual consistency: a GSI may not reflect the most recent writes immediately. That means when your application requires the latest value for a read-after-write scenario, you must design accordingly — for example, perform a strongly consistent read against the base table when necessary, or design the workflow to tolerate slight propagation delay. A practical step: when introducing a GSI for an attribute on existing items, populate the attribute on older items so the index contains complete data. Use GSIs when you cannot predict all access patterns up front or when queries must span partitions, and reserve LSIs for partition-scoped, strongly consistent needs. In practical terms, when to add a gsi and how eventual consistency affects your application. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Global Secondary Index
Definition and behavior
A secondary index with an independent partition and optionally sort key, spanning all table partitions.
  • • Enables queries that can't be expressed with the base table key.
  • • Eventually consistent by default; may lag behind writes briefly.
  • • Can be created or deleted after the table exists and has separate capacity.
Concrete example
If you need to query accounts by status across all users, create a GSI with status as the partition key and price_range or created_at as a sort key.
Operational note
Plan capacity for your GSI or use on-demand. Remember eventual consistency when designing user-facing flows that depend on immediate visibility.
Migration tip
To populate a new GSI for existing items, update items to include the indexed attribute so they appear in the index.

screens.title: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) — architecture and trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB Accelerator, or DAX, is an in-memory caching layer that sits in front of DynamoDB to reduce read latency from milliseconds to microseconds for high-volume, read-heavy workloads. Because DAX is A P I-compatible with DynamoDB, you can often switch clients with minimal code change. DAX is fully managed and highly available, and it handles cache coherence for you, but it does not change the consistency characteristics of the underlying store: reads from the cache are subject to the same eventual consistency trade-offs as many GSIs. DAX is particularly appropriate for repeated reads of hot items where slight staleness is acceptable. It reduces load on the DynamoDB table, potentially lowering consumed read capacity and throttling risk. Misconception: DAX is not a substitute for indexes; it accelerates reads but does not enable new query patterns. Architectural decision: place DAX for read-heavy endpoints and still use GSIs or LSIs to model your queries. Monitor cache hit ratios to determine whether DAX yields cost and latency benefits for your workload. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › DAX Architecture
How DAX fits
DAX sits between your application and DynamoDB to serve cached reads with microsecond latency.
• Reduces read latency for hot items and lowers load on the table.
• API-compatible with DynamoDB clients, enabling easier adoption.
• Best for read-heavy endpoints where eventual staleness is acceptable.
Concrete scenario
Use DAX for a leaderboard or frequently accessed product metadata where speed matters and slightly stale reads are tolerable.
Trade-offs
DAX reduces latency but introduces cache coherence and staleness considerations; it does not remove the need for correct indexing.
Monitoring tip
Track cache hit ratio and DynamoDB consumed capacity; DAX is effective when hit ratios are high and reads dominate traffic.

screens.title: Transactions in practice — transfer funds example
screens.narratorSegment: Transactions give you ACID guarantees across multiple reads and writes in DynamoDB within a single region and account. The classic use case is transferring funds between accounts: you must debit one account and credit another atomically. The provided Python example uses the low-level transact_write_items call to update two account items in a single operation with a condition that ensures sufficient funds. When you run this pattern, a successful transact_write_items call applies both updates; if any condition fails, the whole transaction is canceled and no partial state is applied. That simplifies your application logic because you no longer need compensating actions. A common misconception is that transactions scale like single-item writes; transactions are limited to a small number of items per call and have higher latency and throughput considerations, so use them when atomicity is essential. In practice, group only the items that must be updated together. Also handle TransactionCanceledException to inspect cancellation reasons and guide retry or user feedback. This demo pattern is safe for simple transfers and shows how ConditionExpression protects invariants. Transactions in practice — transfer funds example means use transactions to make grouped updates atomic; handle failures explicitly and keep transaction scope small for performance.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Transactions — Python
Concept
TransactWriteItems groups updates into an all-or-nothing operation with ACID semantics.
Keep transactions limited to the items that must change together. Expect higher latency and design error handling for transaction cancellation reasons.
Example code (excerpt)
import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb', region_name='us-east-1')

def transfer_funds(from_account_id, to_account_id, amount):
  try:
    response = dynamodb.meta.client.transact_write_items(
      TransactItems=[
        {
          'Update': {
            'TableName': 'Accounts',
            'Key': {'account_id': {'S': from_account_id}},
            'UpdateExpression': 'SET balance = balance - :amount',
            'ConditionExpression': 'balance >= :amount',
            'ExpressionAttributeValues': {':amount': {'N': str(amount)}}
          }
        },
        {
          'Update': {
            'TableName': 'Accounts',
            'Key': {'account_id': {'S': to_account_id}},
            'UpdateExpression': 'SET balance = balance + :amount',
            'ExpressionAttributeValues': {':amount': {'N': str(amount)}}
          }
        }
      ]
    )
    return response
  except ClientError as e:
    raise
Concrete example
Transfer 200 from user123 to user456; if the source has insufficient funds the transaction fails and no balances change.
Common mistake
Relying on transactions for bulk updates across many items. Transactions are limited and should be used for small sets of dependent updates.
Key Takeaway
Transactions simplify correctness for coordinated updates, but use them judiciously due to performance limits.

screens.title: Handling transaction failures and ConditionExpression patterns
screens.narratorSegment: When a transaction fails, inspect cancellation reasons and handle them deterministically. One common pattern is to use ConditionExpression to enforce invariants — for example, ensuring a balance is at least the transfer amount before debiting. If the condition fails, DynamoDB raises a TransactionCanceledException and none of the writes are applied. Your application should translate that into a user-facing error or a compensating workflow, not into partial retries that could create duplicates. For transient errors or conditional conflicts, implement retry logic with exponential backoff and idempotency keys where appropriate. A typical retry strategy is to examine the CancellationReasons field to determine if the failure is due to a conditional check or a transient capacity issue. If it's a conditional check, do not retry blindly; surface the issue. If it's a transient capacity problem, back off and retry. Misconception: simply retrying without understanding the reason can cause repeated failures or inconsistent user experiences. Keep transactions narrow and design idempotent, observable handlers for failures. Handling transaction failures and ConditionExpression patterns means distinguish conditional failures from transient errors; retry only when safe, and use idempotency patterns for retries.. In practical terms, designing safe retries and guarding state with conditions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

One common pattern is to use ConditionExpression to enforce invariants — for example, ensuring a balance is at least the transfer amount before debiting. If the condition fails, DynamoDB raises a TransactionCanceledException and none of the writes are applied. Your application should translate that into a user-facing error or a compensating workflow, not into partial retries that could create duplicates. For transient errors or conditional conflicts, implement retry logic with exponential backoff and idempotency keys where appropriate. A typical retry strategy is to examine the CancellationReasons field to determine if the failure is due to a conditional check or a transient capacity issue. If it's a conditional check, do not retry blindly; surface the issue. If it's a transient capacity problem, back off and retry. Misconception: simply retrying without understanding the reason can cause repeated failures or inconsistent user experiences. Keep transactions narrow and design idempotent, observable handlers for failures. Handling transaction failures and ConditionExpression patterns means distinguish conditional failures from transient errors; retry only when safe, and use idempotency patterns for retries.. Use exponential backoff for transient errors and idempotency tokens to avoid duplicate side effects.

screens.title: DynamoDB Streams — event sources for real-time integration
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB Streams provide a time-ordered list of item-level modifications on a table. When enabled, every create, update, or delete produces a stream record that can be consumed by Lambda or other processors to implement event-driven workflows. Typical uses include updating a search index when items change, sending notifications on order status transitions, replicating data to analytics stores, or computing incremental metrics. Streams are partitioned into shards and deliver records in sequence per shard; design your consumers with idempotence and checkpointing so retries and reprocessing are safe. One misconception is expecting a stream to deliver a global total ordering across all partitions — streams ensure ordering per shard, so if your application needs strict ordering across all items, you must add coordination or ordering logic upstream. Streams decouple change capture from the main request path, letting your application keep writes fast while downstream systems perform heavier processing asynchronously. screens.title: Streams + Lambda: an event-driven integration pattern
screens.narratorSegment: A common, practical pattern is to enable DynamoDB Streams and attach a Lambda function to process stream records. Each stream record contains the item's before and after images, enabling your Lambda to update a search index, send notifications, or push changes to an analytics pipeline. Design the Lambda handler to be idempotent: make processing safe to run multiple times for the same record. Use a durable checkpointing mechanism — Lambda integrations manage checkpointing for you when using the supported event source mapping, but if you roll your own consumer, store progress externally. Streams decouple heavy processing from your write path: writes remain fast while downstream jobs handle enrichment or replication. Also design for partial failure: if downstream systems fail, buffer or retry based on backoff and dead-letter strategies. This keeps systems synchronized without blocking customer requests. screens.title: Data modeling and query optimization best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Effective DynamoDB design starts with access patterns: list every query your application needs and design keys and indexes to serve them efficiently. Avoid resorting to Scan on large tables because scans read the entire table and are costly and slow. Prefer Query with a partition key and optional sort key so you only read the items you need. Use GSIs to support new global patterns and LSIs for alternative ordering within a partition when strong consistency is required. When performing updates, use ConditionExpression to enforce business invariants and reduce race conditions. Monitor CloudWatch for consumed capacity and throttled requests; throttling often indicates hot partitions or insufficient capacity. If you identify hot partitions, redesign keys to spread load or introduce sharding strategies. For read-heavy workloads consider DAX to reduce latency, but remember it adds cache coherence considerations. Finally, instrument and test under realistic load so your model and indexes actually perform at scale. These practices keep your application performant and cost-effective as usage grows. Data modeling and query optimization best practices means design for your queries first, then choose keys, indexes, and caching to serve them efficiently; monitor and iterate based on metrics.. In practical terms, start from access patterns, avoid scans, and monitor to prevent hot partitions. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore the advanced capabilities of DynamoDB that let you support complex queries, extreme read performance, and safe multi-item updates. You'll learn when to choose Local Secondary Indexes for alternative sort orders within a partition, and when Global Secondary Indexes let you query by entirely different keys across the table. We'll also examine DynamoDB Accelerator, an in-memory cache for read-heavy workloads, and DynamoDB Transactions for grouping related updates with ACID guarantees. Finally, you'll see how DynamoDB Streams enable event-driven patterns such as search-index updates and real-time analytics. Each section pairs conceptual guidance with concrete examples and a short Python demo pattern. By the end you'll be able to map common access patterns — like finding users by email, transferring funds between accounts, or pushing updates to a search index — to the right DynamoDB feature. A quick misconception check: eventual consistency applies to GSIs and caches like DAX, so if you need immediate strong consistency you will prefer LSIs or specific read strategies. Consider this orientation your roadmap: pick the right index for the access pattern, use DAX for read scale when eventual consistency is acceptable, use transactions when operations must be atomic, and use Streams to integrate DynamoDB into event-driven pipelines.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to identify and implement the right DynamoDB features for common access patterns. First, you'll distinguish Local Secondary Indexes and Global Secondary Indexes and know when to use each, including their consistency and creation constraints. Next, you'll explain when DynamoDB Accelerator is useful and what trade-offs it introduces. You'll also implement transactions to perform all-or-nothing updates across items and handle common transaction failures. Finally, you'll use DynamoDB Streams to trigger downstream processing and apply data modeling practices that avoid expensive scans and prevent hot partitions. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters: for example, adding a GSI to query by email avoids costly scans and makes lookups fast and predictable. A small misconception check: caches like DAX speed reads but do not change your data model; indexes change how you query. These objectives prepare you to both reason about design choices and implement them in Python using Boto3.

In this second objectives panel you'll focus on eventing and modeling: enable and use DynamoDB Streams to power Lambda-driven workflows, and apply data modeling best practices to reduce cost and increase performance. You'll learn to recognize when to use Query instead of Scan to limit input and output, and how to use ConditionExpressions to enforce invariants such as checking balances before debits. You'll also know how to monitor CloudWatch metrics for throttling and hot partitions and take action with GSIs or key design changes. These objectives combine practical steps and monitoring habits so you don't only implement features but also operate them reliably. For example, enabling a stream lets you update a search index on item change rather than batch scanning the table. Misconception check: Streams do not guarantee ordering across partitions, but they do provide a time-ordered sequence per shard; design your processor accordingly. Together these skills will help you build maintainable, scalable DynamoDB-backed services.

Indexes let you query attributes other than the table primary key, but LSIs and GSIs differ in important respects. A Local Secondary Index shares the table partition key and provides a different sort key, so it's local to items that share a partition value and always offers strong consistency with the base table. Because of that close coupling, LSIs must be defined when you create the table. A Global Secondary Index can have an entirely different partition key and sort key, letting queries span the whole table across partitions, and you can add or remove GSIs after table creation. GSIs are by default eventually consistent, and they have separate capacity or on-demand billing configurations. Practically, use an LSI when you need alternative sorting for items within the same partition and you require strong consistency. Use a GSI when you need to support a different access pattern — for example, finding users by email or items by category across the entire dataset. A common misconception is to think GSIs are always a drop-in replacement for LSIs; they are not, because GSIs may return stale results briefly and consume separate capacity. Key decision factors are your access patterns, consistency requirements, and whether you can design keys up front. Think in terms of query needs first, then index to support them.

A Local Secondary Index provides an alternate sort key while keeping the table's partition key. This relationship makes LSIs local to the partition key value, so queries using the LSI only see items that share that partition. Because the index is tightly coupled to the base table, reads through an LSI are strongly consistent with the base table, and changes are reflected immediately for that partition. LSIs are most appropriate when you know you will query items under the same partition in different orderings — for example, storing orders with user_id as partition key and using order_date as an LSI sort key to list a user's orders by date. Remember that LSIs must be created at table creation time, so include them in your initial schema design if you need this behavior. A common design trap is attempting to use an LSI to support queries across partitions; LSIs cannot do that because their partition key is the table partition key. In practice you would model user-scoped queries with LSIs and use GSIs when queries must span all users. Key takeaway: LSIs give immediate, strongly consistent alternate sorting inside a partition, but they require forward schema planning.

A Global Secondary Index gives you the freedom to query a table using a different partition key and sort key than the base table. Because GSIs are global, queries on them can return items from across all partitions, enabling entirely new access patterns such as looking up accounts by status or users by email. GSIs can be added or removed after table creation and have their own capacity or on-demand billing configurations. The trade-off is eventual consistency: a GSI may not reflect the most recent writes immediately. That means when your application requires the latest value for a read-after-write scenario, you must design accordingly — for example, perform a strongly consistent read against the base table when necessary, or design the workflow to tolerate slight propagation delay. A practical step: when introducing a GSI for an attribute on existing items, populate the attribute on older items so the index contains complete data. Use GSIs when you cannot predict all access patterns up front or when queries must span partitions, and reserve LSIs for partition-scoped, strongly consistent needs. Global Secondary Index (GSI) deep dive means gsis let you support different global query patterns but are eventually consistent and have independent capacity considerations.. In practical terms, when to add a gsi and how eventual consistency affects your application. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DynamoDB Accelerator, or DAX, is an in-memory caching layer that sits in front of DynamoDB to reduce read latency from milliseconds to microseconds for high-volume, read-heavy workloads. Because DAX is A P I-compatible with DynamoDB, you can often switch clients with minimal code change. DAX is fully managed and highly available, and it handles cache coherence for you, but it does not change the consistency characteristics of the underlying store: reads from the cache are subject to the same eventual consistency trade-offs as many GSIs. DAX is particularly appropriate for repeated reads of hot items where slight staleness is acceptable. It reduces load on the DynamoDB table, potentially lowering consumed read capacity and throttling risk. Misconception: DAX is not a substitute for indexes; it accelerates reads but does not enable new query patterns. Architectural decision: place DAX for read-heavy endpoints and still use GSIs or LSIs to model your queries. Monitor cache hit ratios to determine whether DAX yields cost and latency benefits for your workload. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) — architecture and trade-offs means dax provides an in-memory cache for microsecond reads, but it complements indexes rather than replacing them and is best for hot, read-heavy access patterns.. In practical terms, how dax fits between your application and dynamodb for microsecond reads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Transactions give you ACID guarantees across multiple reads and writes in DynamoDB within a single region and account. The classic use case is transferring funds between accounts: you must debit one account and credit another atomically. The provided Python example uses the low-level transact_write_items call to update two account items in a single operation with a condition that ensures sufficient funds. When you run this pattern, a successful transact_write_items call applies both updates; if any condition fails, the whole transaction is canceled and no partial state is applied. That simplifies your application logic because you no longer need compensating actions. A common misconception is that transactions scale like single-item writes; transactions are limited to a small number of items per call and have higher latency and throughput considerations, so use them when atomicity is essential. In practice, group only the items that must be updated together. Also handle TransactionCanceledException to inspect cancellation reasons and guide retry or user feedback. This demo pattern is safe for simple transfers and shows how ConditionExpression protects invariants. Transactions in practice — transfer funds example means use transactions to make grouped updates atomic; handle failures explicitly and keep transaction scope small for performance.. In practical terms, a python transact_write_items pattern that ensures atomic debits and credits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a transaction fails, inspect cancellation reasons and handle them deterministically. One common pattern is to use ConditionExpression to enforce invariants — for example, ensuring a balance is at least the transfer amount before debiting. If the condition fails, DynamoDB raises a TransactionCanceledException and none of the writes are applied. DynamoDB Streams provide a time-ordered list of item-level modifications on a table. When enabled, every create, update, or delete produces a stream record that can be consumed by Lambda or other processors to implement event-driven workflows. Typical uses include updating a search index when items change, sending notifications on order status transitions, replicating data to analytics stores, or computing incremental metrics. Streams are partitioned into shards and deliver records in sequence per shard; design your consumers with idempotence and checkpointing so retries and reprocessing are safe. One misconception is expecting a stream to deliver a global total ordering across all partitions — streams ensure ordering per shard, so if your application needs strict ordering across all items, you must add coordination or ordering logic upstream. Streams decouple change capture from the main request path, letting your application keep writes fast while downstream systems perform heavier processing asynchronously. Effective DynamoDB design starts with access patterns: list every query your application needs and design keys and indexes to serve them efficiently. Avoid resorting to Scan on large tables because scans read the entire table and are costly and slow. Prefer Query with a partition key and optional sort key so you only read the items you need. Use GSIs to support new global patterns and LSIs for alternative ordering within a partition when strong consistency is required. When performing updates, use ConditionExpression to enforce business invariants and reduce race conditions. Monitor CloudWatch for consumed capacity and throttled requests; throttling often indicates hot partitions or insufficient capacity. If you identify hot partitions, redesign keys to spread load or introduce sharding strategies. For read-heavy workloads consider DAX to reduce latency, but remember it adds cache coherence considerations. Finally, instrument and test under realistic load so your model and indexes actually perform at scale. These practices keep your application performant and cost-effective as usage grows. These are the core ideas to carry forward. First, Local Secondary Indexes share the table partition key and provide alternate sort keys with strong consistency within a partition. Second, Global Secondary Indexes let you query by different keys across the entire table but are eventually consistent and have separate capacity. Third, DAX is an in-memory cache that accelerates reads for hot, read-heavy workloads but does not change query expressiveness or replace indexes.
